source_reviews.independent_solution: At comparable pressure, cooler air is denser than warmer air. In connected house spaces, buoyancy tends to put cooler air lower and warmer air higher, so warm air does not simply settle into the basement. A basement also normally gains less solar heat and exchanges heat with relatively cool, thermally sluggish surrounding ground. These heat-gain differences and stable thermal stratification explain the usual summer observation; convection alone neither produces cold nor guarantees that every basement is cooler.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Air warmed in the room becomes less dense at similar pressure and rises. source_reviews.independent_solution: Hot chimney gas is less dense than outside air at comparable pressure. If the outlet pressures are approximately equal, the outside column produces a larger pressure rise downward than the hot inside column. Thus the lower inlet has an inward driving pressure difference approximately delta p = g H (rho_out - rho_in) > 0. Increasing H with density contrast and other operating conditions comparable increases this available draft and can draw more replacement air into the combustion equipment. Actual flow also depends on resistance, wind, and gas temperature, so height is not an unconditional guarantee or a source of hotter gas.
